original_multiple_choice.question: A company wants an application running on Amazon EC2 to access objects in an Amazon S3 bucket without storing long-term access keys on the instance. Which option should the company use?

options.text: Create an IAM user and store its access key on the EC2 instance.
Attach an IAM role with the required S3 permissions to the EC2 instance.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced for the S3 bucket.
Store the access key in an Amazon Machine Image.

original_multiple_choice.explanation: The application should use an IAM role attached to the EC2 instance. IAM roles provide temporary credentials and can be scoped to least-privilege permissions for trusted AWS resources.

original_multiple_choice.question: A team wants to receive a notification when monthly AWS spending is forecasted to exceed a configured amount. Which AWS service or feature should they use?
original_multiple_choice.explanation: AWS Budgets can track cost and usage against configured thresholds and send alerts when actual or forecasted spend exceeds those thresholds.

original_multiple_choice.question: A web application must remain available if a single Availability Zone becomes unavailable. Which architecture best meets this requirement?

options.text: Deploy all instances in one Availability Zone and create frequent AMI backups.
Deploy instances across multiple Availability Zones behind a load balancer.
Deploy one larger instance in a public subnet.
Store static files in the instance root volume.

original_multiple_choice.explanation: Deploying across multiple Availability Zones behind a load balancer improves high availability and fault tolerance because traffic can continue to route to healthy targets if one Availability Zone is impaired.
